solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Sun lounger on front of cruise ship

parts.note: on can mean concerning, which is RE

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter, so only the start of cruise is used

parts.note: a liner is a large passenger ship

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker stretches out on a sunbed at the bow of a cruise liner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'front of' takes C from cruise. RE (on, as in 'regarding') + C + LINER (ship).
explanation.definitionFit: A sun lounger is a garden or deck chair whose back tips down, so you can lie back in it.

clue.text: Did more work as artist's model and took a break

definitions.text: Did more work as artist's model

definitions.meaning: rested, a past-tense sense of reposing

explanation.surface: An artist's model sat a second session, then had a rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as re-posed it means posed again; read as one word it means lay at rest.

clue.text: Transport vehicle on railway

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: Goods are moved by rail.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry is to convey from place to place, a verb synonym for transport.

clue.text: Interns must supply scalpels perhaps

indicators.note: supply read as supple-y, in a flexible way, so the letters bend into a new order

explanation.surface: Junior doctors must hand out the surgical blades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' looks like a verb, but read as 'in a supple manner' it signals the rearrangement of INTERNS MUST.
explanation.definitionFit: Scalpels are examples of surgical tools; 'perhaps' marks that they are just one kind.

clue.text: Attract tourists, principally, in eastern Mediterranean resort

indicators.note: in shows one piece placed within the others

parts.note: Nice is a resort on the French Riviera

indicators.note: principally means first and foremost, so the word's first letter is used

explanation.surface: A resort on the Med draws in visitors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'principally' takes T from tourists; 'in' puts it inside E + NICE: E-N-T-ICE.
explanation.definitionFit: To entice is to lure or tempt, a synonym for attract.

clue.text: Healthy food rejected for the most part, unfortunately

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters run backwards
most of the word is kept, with its final letter left off

parts.note: a salad is the classic healthy dish

explanation.surface: Someone sadly reports that their healthy meal was mostly refused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for the most part' cuts SALAD to SALA, and 'rejected' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are expressions of regret said when news is bad, an interjection standing for a sentence adverb.

clue.text: Trio taken short in country road, finding toilet

indicators.note: in shows one piece placed within the other

parts.note: a lane is a narrow country road

indicators.note: cut short, with its last letter removed; 'taken short' is also slang for needing a toilet urgently

explanation.surface: Three walkers, suddenly needing the loo on a country lane, find one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken short' is British slang for urgently needing the toilet, which suits the surface; here it just docks the last letter of Trio before 'in' places it.
explanation.definitionFit: A latrine is a basic toilet, often in a camp or barracks.

clue.text: Youngster getting into humorous programmes

indicators.note: the letters lie inside the run of words that follow

explanation.surface: A child enjoys comedy shows on television.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across humorouS PROGrammes. SPROG is British slang for a child.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprog is an informal British word for a young child.

clue.text: Father joins retired teacher in European capital

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

indicators.note: retired means drawn back, so the word for the teacher is read backwards

parts.note: pupils address a male teacher as sir

explanation.surface: Dad moves in with a former schoolteacher in a European city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' looks like 'no longer working' but signals reading backwards; sir is how British pupils address a male teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: The French capital city is a European capital.

clue.text: Course advisor organised trips covering half term

indicators.note: covering means wrapped around, so the rearranged letters go round the other piece
organised means arranged, so the letters of trips are put into a new order
half of a four-letter word is its first two letters

explanation.surface: A school or travel adviser arranges excursions over half-term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organised' makes TIPSR from trips, and 'covering' wraps it round the first two letters of term. 'Course' is a racecourse, not a school course.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing tipster advises punters on which horse to back at a racecourse, so 'course' means a racecourse.

clue.text: Description of mum, dad, nan and sis, in a word

definitions.text: Description of mum, dad, nan and sis, in a word

parts.words: Description of mum, dad, nan and sis, in a word
parts.note: each family word reads the same forwards and backwards, and one adjective covers them all

explanation.surface: Summing up the family members in a single word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a word' looks like 'briefly' but means each item is a single word with this property.
explanation.definitionFit: Words such as mum and sis read identically in both directions, the defining property of this adjective.

clue.text: Leader of Salvation Army gutted, for instance

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter
a gutted word has lost its insides, leaving only the outside letters

explanation.surface: The head of the Salvation Army is bitterly disappointed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader of' gives S; 'gutted' empties Army to AY. 'Gutted' here is not British slang for upset but literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both introduce an example: 'take, say, Paris' means 'take, for example, Paris'.

clue.text: Remembering the vocation of a teacher of religion?

indicators.note: the vocation belongs to the religion teacher, so the subject comes first

parts.note: RE is religious education, the school subject
a calling is a vocation

explanation.surface: Someone muses on what draws a person to teach religion.
explanation.walkthrough: An RE teacher's vocation is an 'RE calling'. RE is the British school subject Religious Education.
explanation.definitionFit: Recalling something is bringing it back to mind, a straight synonym for remembering.

clue.text: Leave city of London area beset by "rising" problem?

indicators.note: beset by means surrounded by, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: damp is a household problem; 'rising damp' is damp creeping up walls
EC is the postcode area for the City of London

explanation.surface: A householder thinks of moving out of a London flat plagued by rising damp.
explanation.walkthrough: "rising" is in quotes because rising damp (moisture climbing house walls) is the British name for the problem; it decorates the leaf rather than reversing anything.
explanation.definitionFit: To decamp is to depart suddenly, often secretly, so it can stand for leave as a verb.

clue.text: Canadian adolescent in dining room

parts.note: CAN is the abbreviation for Canadian
a teen is an adolescent

explanation.surface: A Canadian teenager sits in the cafeteria.
explanation.definitionFit: A canteen is a dining hall in a school, factory or barracks.

clue.text: Disturbance in Cajun restaurant

indicators.note: in shows the letters sit inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Trouble breaks out at a Louisiana-style eatery.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across cajUN RESTaurant.
explanation.definitionFit: Unrest is agitation or protest in a population, a synonym for disturbance.

clue.text: Eject all those in attendance

definitions.meaning: throw out, as a verb phrase of two words
the number of people who come to an event

explanation.surface: A bouncer throws out everyone at the event.
explanation.definitionFit: As two words it means to expel; as one noun it is the count of people attending.

clue.text: Bride and I distracted, watching this on camera?

indicators.note: distracted means thrown into confusion, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A newly married couple lose focus during the wedding photos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distracted' rearranges BRIDE and I. Photographers say 'watch the birdie' to make people look at the lens.
explanation.definitionFit: The photographer's old catchphrase urges sitters to look at an imaginary bird by the lens.

clue.text: Money expert in more stylish clothing

indicators.note: clothing means dressing, so one word wraps around the other

parts.note: fancier means more elaborate or smarter

explanation.surface: A banker in smarter clothes than usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothing' looks like a noun about garments but works as a verb meaning wrapping round.
explanation.definitionFit: A financier manages large sums of money, so is an expert in finance.

clue.text: Scuffle, with fifty missing trip by plane

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so that letter is taken away

parts.note: a flight is a journey by air
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A brawl breaks out on a flight after fifty passengers go absent.
explanation.definitionFit: A scuffle is a short confused tussle, a kind of fight.

clue.text: Mongrel's successful treatment after losing tail

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its final letter, which is dropped

parts.note: a cure is a treatment that works

explanation.surface: A dog of mixed breed is fully treated by the vet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after losing tail' drops the last letter of CURE.
explanation.definitionFit: A cur is a mixed-breed or worthless dog, so a mongrel.

clue.text: Two businesses introducing a drink

indicators.note: two signals that the abbreviation for a business appears twice

parts.note: CO, for company, is a business

explanation.surface: Two firms launch a new beverage.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocoa is a hot drink made from cacao powder and milk.

clue.text: Assumed visitor is to be announced

indicators.note: announced means spoken out, so the word comes from how the phrase sounds

parts.note: a visitor is a guest, and guest is shortens to guest's

explanation.surface: Someone presumes a caller is about to be introduced at the door.
explanation.definitionFit: To have guessed is to have supposed without proof, a synonym for assumed.

clue.text: Overly masculine Scottish fellow with small house

parts.note: Mac is a familiar address to a Scotsman, from the surname prefix
HO is the abbreviation for house, signalled by small

explanation.surface: A tough-guy Scot lives in a tiny cottage.
explanation.definitionFit: Macho describes aggressively manly behaviour, the excess implied by overly.

clue.text: Taste less than half of small citrus fruit

indicators.note: four of the nine letters is under half, so the rest is cut away

parts.note: a tangerine is a small orange-like fruit

explanation.surface: Someone samples a little piece of a tangerine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'less than half of' keeps four of the nine letters, the opening ones.
explanation.definitionFit: A tang is a sharp, distinctive flavour, a kind of taste.

clue.text: Inclination to write song

parts.note: to pen is to write
a chant is a simple repeated song

explanation.surface: A songwriter feels the urge to compose.
explanation.definitionFit: A penchant is a liking or tendency, a fondness that matches inclination.
